section.title: Seeking Him in the Night
section.sectionRationale: In a short, dreamlike scene the bride wakes in the night to find her beloved gone. She rises, searches the sleeping city, questions the watchmen, and will not rest until she finds him and holds him fast. It is a vivid picture of love that seeks, of the ache of absence, and of the joy of finding, closed once more by the refrain not to awaken love before its time.
section.thesis: Love that has known the beloved cannot rest in his absence; the bride seeks him through the night, finds him, holds him fast, and will not let him go, and the movement closes with the guarding refrain of love’s right time.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the night search, the bride rising to seek the one she loves through the streets until she finds and holds him; and the closing refrain, do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.

units.label: The night search and the finding
units.note: I sought the one I love

verses.text: On my bed at night I sought the one I {{ahav|love}}; I sought him, but did not find him.
I will arise now and go about the city, through the streets and squares. I will seek the one I love. So I sought him but did not find him.
I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city: “Have you seen the one I love?”
I had just passed them when I found the one I love. I held him and would not let go until I had brought him to my mother’s house, to the chamber of the one who conceived me.

units.label: The guarding refrain
units.note: do not awaken love too soon

verses.text: O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken {{ahavah|love}} until the time is right.

ahav.gloss: To love. Four times in this short scene the bride calls the man the one I love, literally the one whom my soul loves. It is a restless, seeking love that cannot settle until it finds him.

ahavah.gloss: Love, the noun from the same root. The closing refrain charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to arouse or awaken love until its proper time, guarding the season of love.

basic.context: In a brief, dreamlike scene the bride wakes at night and reaches for her beloved, but he is not there. She gets up and searches the dark city, asks the watchmen if they have seen him, and just past them she finds him. She takes hold of him and will not let go until she has brought him home. Then comes the refrain again: do not awaken love before its time.
basic.hermeneutics: The scene works by the logic of a dream or longing: absence, restless searching, and the relief of finding. On the plain level it captures how love that has known the beloved cannot rest without him. Read within the whole Bible, it also pictures the soul that seeks God, and the God who lets Himself be found by those who seek Him. The literal ache opens onto the deeper one.
basic.originalLanguages: Over and over the bride names her man the one I love, in Hebrew literally the one whom my soul loves, from the verb ahav. The word tells us this is no shallow attachment but love that reaches from the depths. The refrain uses the noun ahavah, love itself, which must not be awakened before its time.
basic.typology: The seeking soul that will not rest until it finds the beloved pictures the heart that seeks God, and the finding pictures the joy of communion. Scripture promises that those who seek the LORD with all their heart will find Him.
basic.christ: The bride’s cry, I sought him but did not find him, and then, I found the one I love, I held him and would not let go, echoes the longing for Christ and the joy of finding Him. Mary at the empty tomb sought the Lord in the dark and, finding Him, held on. Christ is the One worth seeking through any night.
basic.god: God is a God who can be sought and found. He is not indifferent to the ache of absence; He promises that those who seek Him will find Him when they seek Him with all their heart. He also teaches, through the refrain, that love has its proper time.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 29:13, you will seek Me and find Me when you seek Me with all your heart. Psalm 63:1, my soul thirsts for You in a dry land. John 20:11 to 16, Mary seeks and finds the risen Lord.
basic.oneStory: This little night scene sings of love that cannot rest without the beloved. It points beyond itself to the restless heart that seeks God and the God who lets Himself be found, a longing answered fully in the risen Christ.

context.literary:
This is the shortest movement in the Song, five verses, and it is told wholly in the woman's voice as a memory: 'On my bed at night I sought the one I love.' The tense matters. After the open spring of chapter 2 the poem turns inward and backward, to a night when he was not there, and the poem lets her tell it.

The passage turns on two verbs, seek and find. The verb baqash, 'seek,' falls once in 3:1 and twice in 3:2. The verb matsa, 'find,' is the other half. At 3:1 she 'did not find' him, at 3:2 she again did not find him, and at 3:3 the watchmen 'found' her. Then, at 3:4, comes the line that releases the tension: 'I found the one I love.' The finding is placed after a brief meeting with the guards, 'I had just passed them,' so that the discovery comes just beyond help she did not get.

The movement has the shape of a short story: an empty bed, a resolve, a search, a question to the guards, a finding, a grasp and a homecoming. It ends in the mother's house, and then the refrain, 3:5, speaks to the daughters of Jerusalem in the same words as 2:7. The two refrains frame the section 2:8 to 3:5 as a unit, a day and a night that together hold the central theme of love's pursuit.

The passage has a close sibling in 5:2-8, where the lover knocks, she delays, he is gone, and the watchmen beat her. Placing the two side by side shows that the poet has a pattern for the loss of the beloved and the search for him, and that the first version ends in joy while the second ends with her still seeking. The night in chapter 3 is the gentle one.
context.historical:
In an ancient walled city the night belonged to the watchmen. They walked their rounds on the walls and through the streets, and a woman out alone in the dark would be asked what she was doing and could be in danger. Isaiah speaks of watchmen posted on the walls of Jerusalem who must not be silent day or night, Isaiah 62:6, and the Psalms say that the watchmen stand guard over the city, Psalm 127:1. The bride meets them 'on their rounds,' and the question she asks them is the plain question of someone in distress. The poem's picture of the night city is true to life, and it explains why the bride's act is bold.

The homes of the time were arranged so that the mother's house was a place of honor and safety. A young woman who brought a man to 'my mother's house, to the chamber of the one who conceived me' was bringing him to the center of her family. In Genesis, Isaac brought Rebekah into the tent of his mother Sarah, Genesis 24:67, and in the Song the bride speaks at 8:2 of leading him to the house of the mother who taught her. The mother's house is where a marriage is acknowledged.

The scene of the empty bed also reflects a world in which lovers were not free to meet at will. Betrothed or newly married couples lived under the eyes of families, and a man might be away with the flocks or in the king's service. The poem works with that situation: a lover absent for ordinary reasons, and a woman who will not wait for the morning.

The 'daughters of Jerusalem' are the same chorus as in chapter 1, young women of the city. They listen to the story of her night, and her closing charge is aimed at them, since they are the ones who would be drawn to rouse love early.
context.canonical:
The pattern of seeking and finding is one of the great patterns of the Bible, and this short scene is its love-song form. Moses promises Israel in exile, 'you will seek the LORD your God, you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul,' Deuteronomy 4:29. Jeremiah repeats it, 'You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart,' Jeremiah 29:13. Isaiah says, 'Seek the LORD while He may be found,' Isaiah 55:6, and Jesus says, 'seek, and you will find,' Matthew 7:7. The writer to the Hebrews says that God 'rewards those who earnestly seek Him,' Hebrews 11:6.

The night belongs to this pattern. The psalmists seek God in the dark. 'When I remember You on my bed, I think of You through the watches of the night,' Psalm 63:6, and Isaiah says, 'My soul longs for You in the night,' Isaiah 26:9. The bride's search from her bed uses the same circumstances that the worshiper's longing does.

The New Testament gives the pattern a face. The Gospel of John tells how Mary Magdalene stood weeping by the tomb in the dark and was asked by the risen Jesus, 'Whom are you seeking?' John 20:15. Luke tells of the disciples whose hearts burned as He spoke on the road, Luke 24:32.

The bridal frame is also present. Jesus' parable of the bridegroom has the cry go up 'at midnight,' Matthew 25:6, and the Bible's last chapter has the Spirit and the bride saying 'Come,' Revelation 22:17. The longing for an absent bridegroom is part of how the church lives in the present age, 'though you have not seen Him, you love Him,' 1 Peter 1:8. Jewish and Christian interpreters have read the bride's search as Israel seeking God, or the soul seeking Christ, and the plain sense of a woman seeking her lover is what carries those readings.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet wants the first hearers to understand that love has a cost when the beloved is not there. The bride is not at ease, and she does not wait for the morning. Her words are a lesson in desire that is serious: it will leave the bed, enter the street and ask the guards. The hearers are to see that love is not only a feeling of delight but an active seeking.

The poet also wants to show that such seeking is answered. She does not find him where she searched, but just beyond the guards. The finding does not come from the guards' help, and it does not come at once. It comes after persistence. The hearers were meant to take comfort from that: a love that seeks is not left empty.

Then the poet gives the second lesson. She holds him and does not let go until she has brought him to her mother's house, and then she turns and charges the daughters again, 'Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.' The scene is a picture of strong desire that is tied to home, family and covenant. The poem presents desire as strong and as rightly placed. She does not take him to a hidden place. She takes him to the center of the household.

The repetition of the charge is part of the intent. The poet does not want the hearers to leave with only the thrill of the search. He wants them to hear that love is precious enough to be guarded, and that it is best when it is brought into the open of a family.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The poem describes what the bride did, and it does not command a young woman to wander the city at night. The scene should be read as poetry about the force of longing, not as a model of safe conduct. In 5:7 the same walk ends with the watchmen beating her, so the poem itself shows that the night streets are dangerous. Application should not copy the details.

What the poem does set before the reader is the posture of seeking: she will not be passive, and she asks, and she holds on until she has brought him home. That is a pattern of character that carries over. The believer is urged elsewhere to seek the Lord, Isaiah 55:6, and to pray and not give up. The passage encourages persistence without prescribing the setting.

The refrain in 3:5 is the one explicit instruction, and it is addressed to others, not to the bride herself. It is a wise word that love is not to be hurried, and it belongs with the other times it is said. It is not a command to feel nothing, and it is not a rule about every relationship. It guards the timing of love by calling the hearers to respect its season.

A last point is that the scene may be a dream or a memory, and the text does not insist that it is a plain report of an event. A reader should not build rules from the sequence of events.

debates.question: Is this scene a real event, a dream, or a poetic picture?

views.label: A real event recalled
views.case: The verses are in the past tense, 'I sought him but did not find him,' and are told as a story. The watchmen and the streets are ordinary details, and some readers take the passage as a plain memory.

views.label: A dream
views.case: Many scholars note the dreamlike logic: she wakes or lies in bed, the city is empty, the guards pass her by, and the finding is sudden. The parallel at 5:2, 'I sleep, but my heart is awake,' makes the dream reading attractive, since it places the story at night and in sleep.

views.label: A poetic picture of longing
views.case: Others say that it does not matter whether the scene happened or was dreamed. It is the poet's way of saying that love in absence cannot rest, and the question of whether it is a dream is not one the poem asks.

debates.bearing: The text leaves it open, and a reader does not need to decide. What carries over is the same in all three: the pain of absence, the energy of seeking, and the joy of finding. A caution is that a dream reading should not be pressed so far that the poem becomes only an unreal fancy, for the longing it describes is true to life.

debates.question: Does the scene teach that God can be found, or only that lovers long for each other?

views.label: Only about human love
views.case: The poem never names God in this scene, and the speakers are a woman and a man. Reading it as a picture of the soul seeking God is therefore to bring a meaning to it from outside.

views.label: A picture of the soul seeking God
views.case: Jewish and Christian interpreters have read the scene this way for centuries, pointing to passages like Psalm 63:1 and Jeremiah 29:13, in which the language of seeking and finding is used of God.

views.label: Human love first, and a pattern for seeking God
views.case: On this view the plain sense is real: human love in absence. And because Scripture uses the same language of seeking and finding for God, the scene gives a pattern that the believer may apply to Christ. The application is not a claim that the author hid a code.

debates.bearing: The third view respects the plain sense and the whole Bible. It lets the scene teach about love and then lets it echo in the believer's longing, as long as the application is made with the New Testament's own texts in view.

study.originalLanguages:
The first line, 'On my bed at night I sought,' gives the scene's mood in a few Hebrew words: al mishkavi ballelot, baqashti. The word ballelot looks like a plural, 'in the nights,' and the BSB smooths it to 'at night.' The Hebrew may suggest night after night, a repeated longing, not a single event. The verb baqash, 'to seek,' is the word used of seeking the LORD in other places, as in Deuteronomy 4:29 and Jeremiah 29:13. It is a verb of intention and effort, and its use here sets the bride's search on the same footing as a worshiper's.

The phrase 'the one I love' translates she'ahavah nafshi, literally 'whom my soul loves.' The word nefesh is the whole self: the life, the throat, the appetite, the person. To say that her nefesh loves is to say that her whole being is directed toward him, and the phrase returns four times in these verses, 3:1, 3:2, 3:3 and 3:4. The verb is ahev, the same root as the noun ahavah in the refrain.

The Hebrew of 3:2 begins aqumah na va'asovevah ba'ir, 'I will arise now and go about the city.' The particle na gives the resolve a gentle urgency, as in 'let me arise.' The verb 'go about,' sovev, is the same verb that describes the watchmen, 'the ones going about the city,' 3:3. She goes around the city as they do, and they find her, but she does not find him among them. The verb matsa, 'find,' sets up the play: the watchmen 'found' her, matsa'uni, and she then 'found' him, matsati, at 3:4. The same verb is used for both, as though the night's reversal were a pun.

The verb for her grasp, ahaztiv, 'I held him,' is a verb of firm holding, as in taking possession of something. She adds velo arpennu, 'and I would not let him go,' with the verb raphah, which means to loosen or slacken. The pair says that she held and did not slacken her grip. The same verb raphah appears in Joshua 1:5, where God says 'I will never leave you nor forsake you,' in the sense of not letting go, though the Song uses a different form. It is worth noticing that the grip of her love is like the grip of God's faithfulness in the Bible's wider speech.

The phrase 'my mother's house, the chamber of the one who conceived me,' uses beit immi and cheder horati. The word cheder is an inner room, and horah is a participle of the verb for conceiving. Both words are about the innermost place, and the repetition of 'mother' gives the destination a note of belonging. Finally, the refrain at 3:5 is as at 2:7, with the verbs ta'iru and te'orerru, to rouse and to awaken, and ad shetechpatz, 'until it pleases.' The Song uses the refrain three times, 2:7, 3:5 and 8:4, and only the first two have the oath by the gazelles and does.

typology.fulfillment: The bride's seeking pictures the heart that seeks God in the dark. The psalmist says, 'My soul thirsts for God, the living God,' Psalm 42:2, and 'my soul longs for You in the night,' Isaiah 26:9. The New Testament answers with a Christ who says, 'seek, and you will find,' Matthew 7:7. The escalation is that the God who is sought is also the God who seeks, since the Son of Man came 'to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10. The type falls short because in the Song the lover is only absent, while Christ seeks even when the seeker has not begun.

'I held him and would not let go.' On Easter morning, Mary Magdalene seeks the Lord at the tomb and finds Him, John 20:11-16, and the other women 'grasped His feet, and worshiped Him,' Matthew 28:9. The correspondence is of love that clings to its found beloved. The escalation is a surprising one: Jesus tells Mary, 'Do not cling to Me,' John 20:17, because the relationship is about to change, and the believer is to hold Him now by faith. The type falls short because the bride holds him in her own mother's house, while the church is held by Christ.

typology.type: The watchmen who do not have him
typology.fulfillment: The watchmen in the city know nothing of her beloved, and she passes them to find him. The prophets are posted as watchmen, Isaiah 62:6, and the church has leaders who watch over souls. But the watchmen cannot give the beloved. The correspondence is that every human guide points beyond itself, and the escalation is that John the Baptist, the friend of the bridegroom, says, 'That joy is mine, and it is now complete,' John 3:29, because he points to Christ and steps back. The type falls short because the Song's watchmen are only passed, while the church's guides are servants of the Shepherd.

study.christ:
The Song does not name Christ, and the link has to be drawn with care, but the Bible gives good grounds for it. The scene is the story of a bride and a bridegroom, and Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom, saying that the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them and then they will fast, Matthew 9:15. That is the situation of the bride in 3:1: the bridegroom is away and she longs. The church lives in that same period, and the New Testament describes its mood in words close to the Song's: 'Though you have not seen Him, you love Him,' 1 Peter 1:8.

The strongest New Testament echo is the scene at the tomb. Mary Magdalene comes in the dark to find the body of her Lord. She weeps, she asks the angels, she asks the man she takes for the gardener, 'tell me where you have put Him, and I will get Him,' John 20:15. Then Jesus says her name, and she turns, John 20:16. The pattern is the same: darkness, seeking, a stranger, and a finding that arrives where it is not expected. The Gospel does not claim to be quoting the Song, so the connection is a pattern and not a prophecy. But the match is close enough to hear.

The scene also shows what Christ's love does with the seeking. 'Whom are you seeking?' Jesus asks Mary, John 20:15. He is there before she finds Him. The bride in the Song believes that she found her beloved, and the New Testament adds that the beloved had come looking for her. The Lord says that He came to seek and to save the lost, Luke 19:10, and that the shepherd goes after one lost sheep until he finds it, Luke 15:4. The longing of the believer for Christ is always an answer to His longing for the believer.

The scene gives words to the church's present condition. Between the cross and the return there are nights. The believer may seek and not find, and the Song does not hide this. But it shows that seeking is the right thing to do, and it ends with a finding. 'Come to Me,' Jesus says, Matthew 11:28, and the believer's holding on is what faith looks like. Hebrews says that God 'rewards those who earnestly seek Him,' Hebrews 11:6.

One boundary: it is not right to turn every detail, the watchmen, the streets, the mother's house, into a code for Christ. The movement as a whole is what carries over, the pattern of absence, search and finding, and Christ is the one in whom the search ends.
study.god:
The scene is a picture of human love, but it throws light on what Scripture says of God, and the light is plain. God is first a God who can be sought. The bride's search is not a mistake and it is not in vain. The Lord says through Moses that Israel will find Him if they seek Him with all their heart and soul, Deuteronomy 4:29, and Proverbs gives the wisdom's voice, 'those who seek me early shall find me,' Proverbs 8:17. A doctrine of God that makes Him unreachable has no room for these promises. The God of the Bible is hidden at times, and He is not hiding in order to avoid being found.

God is also a God who permits the dark. The poem does not hide that there is a night in which the beloved is not found at once, and the Bible does not hide it either. The psalmists complain of seeking God in the night, Psalm 63:6, and Isaiah's prayer is a prayer from the night, Isaiah 26:9. The sense of absence does not prove that God is gone. It is part of the way He trains desire, and the poem shows desire being made stronger by the delay.

Third, God is faithful to those who hold on. She does not let go until she has brought him home. The Bible says the same of God's side: He does not abandon those who seek Him, and He promises, 'I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you,' John 14:18. The believer's grip is a response to a hold that is firmer.

A tension that the passage holds is between presence and absence. The believer lives by faith, not by sight, and yet the Lord is near. Neither side is meant to cancel the other. For worship, the passage makes a place for honest longing. The church may sing of its desire for God and not pretend that it is already satisfied, and the Psalms show this: 'As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God,' Psalm 42:1.

Finally, God teaches order. The refrain at the close reminds the hearer that love has its time, and that the God who stirs desire also sets its season. The believer who waits for God's timing is not being denied. The Song says as much about human love, and the Bible says it of God's promises, which come in the fullness of time.

crossReferences.note: The twin of this scene. The lover knocks in the night, she delays, he is gone, and she searches and meets the watchmen, who beat her. The comparison shows that the poet has two versions of the lost beloved, and that 3:1-5 is the one in which the search ends in finding.

She would 'lead you and bring you to the house of my mother who taught me.' The wish of 8:2 is the same as the act of 3:4. The bringing of the beloved to the mother's house is a recurring picture of love brought into the family.

'Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah and took Rebekah as his wife.' This is the closest scene in Genesis to the bringing home in 3:4, and it shows that a bridegroom's mother's tent was the place where a marriage was set. The Song's bride does the same, with the roles turned.

'You will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul.' This is the promise behind the Song's seeking, spoken to Israel in exile. The bride seeks with her soul, nafshi, and finds, and the verse shows that the same pattern is God's word to those who seek Him.

'You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.' The promise to the exiles is put in the same terms of seeking and finding. It is a word of hope for those who feel the absence of God and want Him.

'My soul longs for You in the night; indeed, my spirit seeks You at dawn.' The prophet's prayer has the same setting, longing at night, as the bride's. It shows that the night search is not only a lover's act but a believer's, and that the soul's longing is a common thread.

'Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You.' The psalmist uses the verb for seeking and the word for soul that the bride uses. The psalm moves, as the Song does, from thirst to satisfaction, and it makes the Song's longing a pattern for prayer.

'Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near.' The invitation joins the promise that He may be found with a call to seek now. The Song's bride is a picture of someone who does not delay.
'Seek, and you will find.' Jesus gives the bride's pattern as a promise to those who ask. The finding is not left to chance, and the Lord invites the persistence the poem shows.

Mary stands weeping by the tomb and seeks the Lord, who asks, 'Whom are you seeking?' She turns when He says her name. The scene is the New Testament's nearest echo of the bride's night search, with the added fact that the one sought is already standing near.

God 'rewards those who earnestly seek Him.' The writer treats seeking as a mark of faith. The bride's persistence through the dark is an illustration of what it is to believe that He exists and that the search will be answered.

'At midnight the cry rang out: Here is the bridegroom!' In the parable the night is the time of waiting, and the bridegroom's coming is sudden. It gives the Song's night scene a place in Jesus' teaching about waiting for the bridegroom.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a man and a woman who walked with God in the cool of the day, and then hid, and were sent out. After that, the whole history is a history of seeking: God seeks the lost, and the lost are taught to seek God. 'Where are you?' is the first question God asks in Scripture, Genesis 3:9, and the answer that humanity gave was to hide. The prophets later tell exiles that they will seek and find, Deuteronomy 4:29, Jeremiah 29:13. The Song of Songs puts that longing in the form of a woman in the night.

The night search has a place in the story of the fall because absence is the condition after Eden. The bride does not have what she wants, and she does not rest. That is how the creation itself is described in Romans, as groaning, Romans 8:22. The believer lives in a world where the beloved is sometimes out of sight, and the Song does not say that this is a mistake. It says that it is a night, and nights end.

The story of redemption brings the end of the night in the person of Christ. On the first day of the week, early, while it was still dark, Mary came to the tomb. The one she sought was alive and was already looking for her, John 20:1, 20:15. The Gospel shows that the long search of humanity has an answer, and that the answer has a name. The apostles then say that the church holds this Lord by faith, not yet by sight, 1 Peter 1:8, and that He will come back to take His people to Himself, John 14:3.

The story ends in a wedding and a city. 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man,' says the voice in Revelation, and 'He will wipe away every tear,' Revelation 21:3-4. The night search of the Song is answered when the bride is brought into the house of the Bridegroom and the search is over. There is no more going about the city in the dark.

For the reader, the passage gives language to the middle of the story. The church is between the finding at the tomb and the wedding supper, and it prays, 'Come,' Revelation 22:17. The bride's refusal to let go until she is home is a picture of the believer's persistence, and her closing charge is a reminder that the best things are given in their time. The Song's little night is the Bible's long night, and it is told in the confidence that the Beloved is worth the search.

quiz.q: What happens in the bride’s night scene in 3:1 to 4?

options.text: She wakes to find her beloved gone, searches the city, and at last finds him and holds him fast.
options.note: The arc is absence, seeking, and the joy of finding.

options.text: She dreams of a feast and forgets her beloved.
options.note: Her whole concern is seeking the one she loves; she never forgets him.

options.text: She refuses to look for him and stays in bed.
options.note: The scene does begin with her on her bed at night, but she then rises and searches the streets until she finds him.

options.text: She finds him at once without any searching.
options.note: She does find her beloved and hold him fast, but only after seeking and not finding him for a time through the city.

quiz.q: How does the bride refer to her beloved throughout the scene?

options.text: The one I love, literally the one whom my soul loves, a love from the depths.
options.note: The repeated phrase marks love that reaches from the soul.
She does seek him as one who is absent, but he is no stranger; he is the one her soul loves, deeply known and longed for.

options.text: A rival she wishes to avoid.
options.note: She seeks him urgently, longing to be with him, not to avoid him.

options.text: One of the watchmen of the city.
options.note: The watchmen do appear in the scene, but he is not one of them; they are the ones she questions while searching for him.

quiz.q: What does the scene picture when read within the whole Bible?

options.text: The soul that seeks God in the dark and the God who lets Himself be found.
options.note: Scripture promises that those who seek the LORD wholeheartedly will find Him.

options.text: That God cannot be found no matter how one seeks.
options.note: The opposite: she finds him, and God promises to be found by seekers.

options.text: That seeking God is pointless and one should stay passive.
options.note: The scene is about seeking, but it commends earnest seeking that is rewarded with finding, not passivity.

options.text: Only a ghost story with no spiritual meaning.
options.note: It truly voices human love and longing in its own right, but within the whole canon it also pictures the soul seeking God, so it is more than a ghost story.

quiz.q: What is the refrain that closes the scene in 3:5?

options.text: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.
options.note: The guarding refrain sounds again, honoring love’s proper season.

options.text: Never seek the one you love.
options.note: The refrain does counsel restraint, holding love back until its time, but the scene commends seeking; it does not forbid seeking the one you love.

options.text: Love should be awakened as early as possible.
options.note: The refrain says the opposite, do not awaken love before its time.

options.text: The watchmen alone can find true love.
options.note: The watchmen do appear earlier in the scene, but the refrain is about love’s right time, not about the watchmen finding love.

questions: The bride cannot rest while her beloved is absent. Have you known a restlessness for God that would not settle until you drew near to Him again?
She rose in the night and searched the streets rather than waiting passively. What would it look like for you to actively seek the Lord in a season when He feels distant?
I held him and would not let go, she says. Where do you need to take hold of Christ and refuse to let a hardship pull you from Him?
God promises that those who seek Him with all their heart will find Him. What might be dividing your heart and dulling your search for Him?
The refrain again guards the right time of love. Where are you tempted to force something before its season, and how might patient trust change that?

translationNotes.note: The one I love renders a Hebrew phrase, the one whom my soul loves, stressing love from the depths of the person.
The scene reads like a dream or nighttime reverie; its logic is longing and seeking rather than strict narrative.
The refrain, do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right, recurs at 2:7 and 8:4.
